Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem: combining efficient fine-tuning with low-bit inference. Quantizing the combined base weights and LoRA update provides a plausible way to eliminate the separate adapter path without QA-LoRA’s structural restrictions.

Evaluation covers several model families and sizes from 3B to 33B, two bit widths, and multiple language benchmarks. Some improvements are substantial: at 3 bits, LLaMA-2 7B achieves 61.3% CSQA accuracy versus 57.6% for QLoRA* and 57.9% for OmniQuant.

The paper measures practical resource costs alongside accuracy. Reported 7B training memory is 25.4 GB, close to LoRA’s 25.1 GB and substantially below QAT’s 79.5 GB. Kernel-based inference measurements support the benefit of removing the separate adapter path.
Initialization, rank, and quantization-group ablations provide useful supporting evidence, and the appendices report detailed task results and several training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central efficiency comparison needs better experimental controls. Appendix D uses 25K iterations for L4Q versus 50K for PTQ-based methods, while only L4Q’s 33B model uses sequence length 128 instead of 2048. Different schedules can be justified, but training loss alone does not establish comparable cost at matched validation quality. The sequence-length difference particularly confounds the 33B memory and timing comparisons.

The custom backward pass is not specified unambiguously. Equations 29–30 place a weight-shaped clipping condition outside products producing adapter-shaped gradients. With G=dL/dWq and a weightwise clipping mask M, the gradients should be alpha B^T(G⊙M) and alpha(G⊙M)A^T. This may be a notation error, but the manuscript provides no L4Q implementation link or gradient-validation evidence to resolve it. Microbatch size, gradient accumulation, and checkpointing settings are also missing; the relationship between Figure 3’s 100 steps and Appendix B’s 12,800 iterations is unexplained.

The adapted baselines require stronger validation. Uniform quantization is a reasonable controlled setting and is explicitly disclosed, but LoftQ* collapses to approximately chance-level MMLU performance in many 3-bit experiments without adequate diagnosis. Quantizer initialization and baseline hyperparameter-selection procedures need documentation. A fine-tune, merge, then PTQ baseline would also help establish the benefit over a simpler route to fully quantized inference.

The explanation of the memory advantage does not adequately separate implementation choices from the proposed model structure. Computing and discarding weight gradients locally could also be implemented for QAT-LoRA with frozen base weights. A comparably optimized baseline or memory-component ablation is needed to establish why the reported gap follows from L4Q’s integration.

Several claimed accuracy advantages are too small to assess without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates—for example, 62.7 versus 62.6 on 4-bit LLaMA-1 7B CSQA. Superiority is also not universal: 3-bit LLaMA-2 13B obtains 50.0 on five-shot MMLU versus QLoRA*’s 50.6. The contribution is promising, but the experimental-control and reproducibility concerns require important, plausibly next-cycle revisions before a clear Findings recommendation.
